decks.title: Dissolution of a Partnership Firm — Part 1: Meaning, Section 48 and the Realisation Account
goals: Distinguish dissolution of the partnership from dissolution of the firm
Settle accounts in the order laid down by Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932
Prepare a Memorandum Balance Sheet and transfer balances to the Realisation Account under the ISC rules
Apply the ISC assumptions when the question is silent about an asset or a liability

slides.heading: Dissolution of a Partnership Firm
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what dissolution means, **Section 48**, the **Memorandum Balance Sheet** and what goes to the **Realisation Account**. Every firm, person and figure in this chapter is imagined.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: whether the partnership or the firm is dissolved, settlement under section forty-eight, the memorandum balance sheet, what is transferred to the realisation account, and the assumptions for silent items
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: So far the firm has always carried on: partners joined, retired or changed their shares, and we adjusted the books. In this chapter the business itself comes to an end. We sell the assets, pay the outside liabilities and settle with the partners until every account is closed. This first part covers the meaning of dissolution, the legal order of settlement and how the balances reach the realisation account.

slides.heading: Partnership or firm: what is dissolved?
bullets: **Dissolution of partnership:** the old agreement ends; the firm continues with adjusted books.
**Dissolution of the firm:** the relation among all partners ends; the business closes and the books are closed.

rows: The old agreement among the partners
The relation among **all** partners and the business
Closed: Realisation, capital and Bank/Cash accounts
Admission, retirement, death, change in ratio
All partners agree to close; the court orders winding up
May happen without dissolving the firm

visual.alt: Table comparing dissolution of partnership, where only the old agreement ends and the business continues with adjusted books, with dissolution of the firm, where the relation among all partners and the business end and the books are closed

slides.narration: Two ideas sound alike but differ. When a partner joins, retires or dies, or the ratio changes, the old partnership agreement ends, yet the firm carries on and we simply adjust the books. When the firm itself is dissolved, the relation among all the partners ends, the business stops and every account is closed. Dissolving the firm always dissolves the partnership, but not the other way round.

slides.narration: Ask one question each time: does the business carry on? A retirement, an admission and a change in ratio all leave the business running under a new agreement, so only the partnership is dissolved. When every partner agrees to wind up and sell the assets, the business ends, so the firm is dissolved.

slides.heading: Settlement of accounts under Section 48
bullets: **Losses** first come out of profits, then capital, then the partners personally in the profit-sharing ratio.
The **cash** then pays: third parties → partners' loans → partners' capitals → any residue in the profit-sharing ratio.

nodes.label: Losses (incl. capital deficiency): from profits, then capital, then partners in profit-sharing ratio

visual.alt: Flow of section forty-eight: losses are met from profits, then capital, then by the partners in the profit-sharing ratio; the assets then pay third-party debts, partners loans, partners capitals, and any residue is divided in the profit-sharing ratio
visual.caption: Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932

slides.narration: Section forty-eight of the Indian Partnership Act gives the order of settlement. Losses, including any shortfall of capital, are met first out of profits, then out of capital, and finally by the partners themselves in their profit-sharing ratio. The money is then paid out in a fixed order: outside creditors first, then loans from partners, then partners capitals, and anything left over is shared like profit.

rows: 3. Oishee's capital less 3/5 of the loss
3. Pratyush's capital less 2/5 of the loss

visual.alt: Table of worked example two: claims of 2,60,000 against cash of 2,40,000 give a loss of 20,000, shared three to two; creditors and Pratyush's loan are paid in full, then Oishee 58,000 and Pratyush 42,000
visual.caption: Loss = ₹2,60,000 − ₹2,40,000 = ₹20,000: Oishee ₹12,000, Pratyush ₹8,000.

slides.narration: The claims add up to rupees two lakh sixty thousand, but only rupees two lakh forty thousand is available, so the loss is rupees twenty thousand. Shared three to two, Oishee bears rupees twelve thousand and Pratyush rupees eight thousand. Creditors and Pratyush's loan are paid in full. Oishee then receives rupees fifty-eight thousand and Pratyush rupees forty-two thousand, which uses up the cash exactly.

slides.heading: The Memorandum Balance Sheet
bullets: A **Memorandum Balance Sheet** sets out every balance on the date of dissolution, in **horizontal** form.
It is a statement, not an account: it often reveals a **missing figure** such as cash or a capital.

nodes.label: Ledger balances on the date of dissolution
Missing figure found as the balancing amount
Starting point for Realisation, capital and Bank/Cash accounts

visual.alt: Flow: ledger balances on the date of dissolution are set out in a memorandum balance sheet in horizontal form; a missing figure such as cash or a capital is found as the balancing amount; the statement is the starting point for the realisation, capital and bank or cash accounts
visual.caption: Memorandum Balance Sheet

slides.narration: Before closing the books we need a clear picture of what must be closed. A memorandum balance sheet lists every balance on the date of dissolution, liabilities and capitals on the left and assets on the right. It is only a statement, not part of the double entry, and it is handy when one figure, such as the cash or a partner's capital, is missing.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding the missing cash
slides.body_md: Sohra Umbrella Works (imagined): Banalata and Ishfaq list their balances on the date of dissolution, but the cash in hand is not given.

visual.alt: Memorandum balance sheet of Sohra Umbrella Works totalling 1,42,000: creditors, bills payable, Ishfaq's loan, general reserve and two capitals on the left; machines, stock, debtors and cash in hand of 26,000 found as the balancing figure on the right
visual.caption: Memorandum Balance Sheet of Banalata and Ishfaq (imagined) on the date of dissolution.

slides.narration: The liabilities and capitals total rupees one lakh forty-two thousand. The machines, stock and debtors come to less than that, so the difference, rupees twenty-six thousand, must be the cash in hand. With every balance known, the books are ready to be closed.

slides.heading: The Realisation Account
columns:
**Debit (To)**

- Assets at book (gross) value
- Cash paid for liabilities
- Expenses borne by the firm
- Profit (balancing figure)

**Credit (By)**

- Related provisions and funds
- Outside liabilities
- Cash and takeovers for assets
- Loss (balancing figure)

rows: Assets other than cash/bank, at book (gross) value
Provisions and funds related to those assets
Cash paid for outside liabilities (incl. bank loan)
Outside liabilities at book value (incl. bank loan)
Realisation expenses borne by the firm
Cash from assets sold (recorded and unrecorded)
Liabilities or expenses paid by a partner (his capital)
Assets taken over by partners (their capitals)

visual.alt: Table of the realisation account format: the debit side holds assets at gross book value, cash paid for liabilities, expenses, liabilities paid by partners, unrecorded liabilities and any profit; the credit side holds related provisions and funds, liabilities, cash from assets, assets taken over by partners and any loss

slides.narration: The realisation account is a nominal account that shows whether winding up made a profit or a loss. Assets go on the debit side at their full book value, and anything the firm pays out for liabilities or expenses joins them. The credit side receives the outside liabilities, related provisions and funds, and whatever the assets fetch. The balance is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

slides.heading: What goes where: the ISC rules
slides.body_md: A provision or fund **related** to an asset or liability follows it into the Realisation Account.

headers: Balance on the date of dissolution
rows: Assets (except cash/bank, loan to a partner, fictitious assets)
Realisation A/c, debit, at gross value
Provision or fund **related** to an asset or liability (doubtful debts, depreciation, investment fluctuation)
Bank/Cash A/c (opening credit balance); not to Realisation
Partner's Loan A/c; repaid through Bank/Cash
Debited to that partner's Capital A/c
General reserve, credit balance of profit and loss
Debit balance of profit and loss, advertisement suspense

visual.alt: Table of where each balance goes on dissolution under the ISC syllabus: assets at gross value, related provisions and funds, outside liabilities and bank loans go to the realisation account; a bank overdraft goes to the bank or cash account; partners loans are repaid in cash; loans to partners are debited to their capitals; reserves, accumulated losses and current accounts go to the capital accounts

slides.narration: The syllabus is precise about where each balance goes. Assets go to realisation at their gross value, and any provision or fund related to them goes there too. A bank loan is an outside liability and goes to realisation, but a bank overdraft is closed through the bank account. Partners loans, loans to partners, reserves and current accounts all stay out of realisation.

slides.heading: When the question is silent
bullets: Intangible assets, accrued income, prepaid expenses: **nil**.

visual.alt: Table of the ISC assumptions for silent items: a tangible asset or investments realise book value; intangible assets, accrued income and prepaid expenses realise nothing; a liability is paid in full

slides.narration: Questions often leave some items unmentioned, and the syllabus tells us what to assume. A tangible asset or investments are taken to realise their book value. Intangible assets such as goodwill or patents, accrued income and prepaid expenses are taken to realise nothing. A liability that is not mentioned is paid in full.

slides.narration: To sum up: the firm is dissolved only when the business closes. Section forty-eight meets losses from profits, then capital, then the partners, and pays creditors, partners loans and capitals in that order. A memorandum balance sheet sets out the balances. Assets, related funds and outside liabilities go to realisation, the overdraft goes to the bank account, and silent items follow the syllabus assumptions.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **gross** values of assets in the Realisation Account and credit the provision separately.
Send a fund or provision **related** to an asset or liability to Realisation; send an unrelated reserve to the **capitals**.
**Bank overdraft** opens the Bank A/c; **bank loan** goes through Realisation.
State each **assumption** for silent items in a working note: it earns the step mark.
Never transfer cash, bank, partners' loans or capitals to the Realisation Account.
slides.narration: A few habits save marks. Show assets at their gross value and credit the provision on its own. Remember that related funds go to realisation but a general reserve goes to the capitals. Keep the overdraft in the bank account and the bank loan in realisation. Write down every assumption you make for silent items, and never send cash or partners balances to realisation.

visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: With the balances transferred, the real work of winding up begins. Assets are sold or taken over, liabilities are paid or settled with assets, unrecorded items turn up, and someone pays the expenses. Finally we close the partners accounts and the bank account. We finish the Kamalabari example along the way.

slides.heading: Selling assets and paying liabilities

rows: Bank/Cash A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c
Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank/Cash A/c
Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank/Cash A/c
No entry (its book value stays on the debit side)
Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank/Cash A/c (amount actually paid)

visual.alt: Table of entries for realising assets and paying liabilities: cash from an asset is debited to bank and credited to realisation; liabilities and a bank loan paid are debited to realisation; an asset that realises nothing needs no entry; a discounted settlement is entered at the cash paid

slides.narration: When an asset is sold, the bank is debited and the realisation account credited. When a liability is paid, the realisation account is debited and the bank credited, with the amount actually paid, so a discount simply reduces the debit. An asset that fetches nothing needs no entry at all: its book value already sits on the debit side.

slides.heading: Partners and creditors who take assets
slides.body_md: Only cash that actually moves is entered when a creditor accepts an asset.

rows: Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c (agreed value)
Partner agrees to pay a liability
Realisation A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c
Creditor accepts an asset in full settlement
Creditor accepts an asset and cash for the rest
Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank/Cash A/c (cash part only)

visual.alt: Table of entries when partners or creditors take assets: a partner taking an asset is debited at the agreed value; a partner paying a liability is credited; a creditor accepting an asset in full settlement needs no entry; if he also gets cash, only the cash is entered

slides.narration: A partner who takes over an asset is debited with its agreed value, and realisation is credited. A partner who agrees to pay a liability is credited, and realisation is debited. When a creditor accepts an asset in full settlement, both are already in the realisation account, so no entry is needed. If the creditor also gets some cash, only that cash is entered.

sections.heading: 1. Dissolution of partnership and dissolution of the firm
sections.body_md:
**Dissolution of partnership** ends the existing agreement among the partners, but the firm continues: admission, retirement, death and a change in the profit-sharing ratio all reconstitute the firm, and its books are adjusted.

**Dissolution of the firm** ends the relation of partnership among **all** the partners. The business closes; the assets are realised, the liabilities paid and the partners settled, so every account in the books is closed.

A dissolution of the firm always dissolves the partnership; a dissolution of the partnership need not dissolve the firm.

*Not in the ISC 2027 syllabus for this chapter:* admission-cum-retirement, amalgamation of firms, conversion or sale to a company, piecemeal distribution and insolvency of partners.

sections.heading: 3. The Memorandum Balance Sheet
sections.body_md:
A **Memorandum Balance Sheet** is the firm's balance sheet drawn up on the date of dissolution, in **horizontal** form, to set out the balances that must now be closed. It is a statement, not an account, and is not part of the double entry.

It is useful when the question gives ledger balances in a list, or when one figure (often **cash/bank** or a **partner's capital**) is missing: the missing figure is the balancing amount.

**Check:** total liabilities and capitals = total assets.

sections.heading: 4. The Realisation Account and the ISC rules for transfers
sections.body_md:
The **Realisation Account** is a nominal account opened on dissolution to find the profit or loss on realising the assets and settling the outside liabilities.

**Transfer entries**
- Realisation A/c Dr. To each asset A/c (gross book value; not cash, bank, a loan to a partner or fictitious assets).
- Related provision or fund A/c Dr., outside liability A/cs Dr. To Realisation A/c.

**ISC 2027 rules**
- A fund or reserve **related** to an asset or liability taken to Realisation is also transferred to Realisation, not to capitals (e.g. provision for doubtful debts, provision for depreciation, investment fluctuation fund).
- **Bank overdraft** is taken to the Bank/Cash A/c, not to Realisation; a **bank loan** is transferred to Realisation.

**Silent items (ISC assumptions)**
- Tangible assets and investments: realised at **book value**.
- Intangible assets, accrued income, prepaid expenses: realise **nil**.
- Liabilities: paid **in full**.

key_terms.definition_md: Nominal account recording the transfer, sale and settlement of assets and outside liabilities on dissolution; its balance is the profit or loss on realisation.
A balance set aside against a particular asset or liability; it follows that item into the Realisation Account.

sections.heading: 7. Loans, current accounts, capital accounts and the Bank/Cash Account
sections.body_md:
**Order of closing:** current accounts → reserves and accumulated losses → loan to a partner → realisation result → partners' loans repaid → cash brought in for debit balances → final payment.

- **Current accounts (fixed capitals):** balances transferred to the capital accounts; no adjustment passes through them.
- **General reserve, credit balance of profit and loss:** Reserve A/c Dr. To Partners' Capital A/cs.
- **Debit balance of profit and loss, advertisement suspense:** Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To the account.
- **Loan to a partner:** Partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Loan to Partner A/c.
- **Loan from a partner:** Partner's Loan A/c Dr. To Bank/Cash A/c — even if his capital account has a debit balance (no set-off).
- **Debit balance of capital:** Bank/Cash A/c Dr. To Partner's Capital A/c (cash brought in).
- **Final payment:** Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Bank/Cash A/c.
- **Bank overdraft:** opening credit balance of the Bank A/c (By Balance b/d), cleared from the cash realised.

**Check:** every capital account and the Bank/Cash Account close at **nil**.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Transferring a related fund (investment fluctuation fund, provision) to the capitals instead of the Realisation Account, or a general reserve to Realisation.
- Sending the **bank overdraft** to Realisation; under ISC it opens the Bank/Cash Account. The **bank loan** does go to Realisation.
- Showing debtors net of the provision in the Realisation Account; transfer the **gross** figure and credit the provision.
- Making an entry when a creditor accepts an asset in full settlement.
- Debiting the Realisation Account with expenses that a partner must bear.
- Setting off a partner's loan against a debit balance in his capital account.
- Forgetting the ISC assumptions for silent items (tangible at book value; intangible, accrued and prepaid items nil; liabilities in full).

**How marks are usually awarded (SOYL chapter tests on the ISC default pattern)**
- 1 mark: objective items.
- 2 marks: two or three journal entries, a Memorandum Balance Sheet, or a distinction.
- 3 marks: a Realisation Account, a Section 48 payout, a Bank Account, or capital accounts.
- 5 marks in parts, e.g. (a) 2 + (b) 3: entries and a Realisation Account, or a Realisation Account with capital and Bank accounts.
- Full practical (practice, 8 marks): Realisation Account about 4, capital accounts about 3, Bank/Cash Account about 1–2; working notes for assumptions earn step marks. The ISC 2027 weightage for Dissolution in Paper I is 8 marks.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: Which of these events at Tulunadu Cashew Processors, an imagined three-partner firm at Bantwal, brings the firm itself to an end, and not merely the old partnership agreement?

options.text_md: One partner retires and the other two carry on the cashew business
All three partners agree to close the cashew business, sell its assets and settle its accounts
A fourth partner is admitted and the business continues
The three partners change their profit-sharing ratio from the next year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** All three partners agree to close the cashew business, sell its assets and settle its accounts. Retirement, admission and a change in ratio only reconstitute the firm, which carries on with adjusted books. When the business is closed and every account settled, the firm itself is dissolved.

questions.stem_md: When Hoysala Granite Polishers, an imagined firm at Belur, is wound up, the cash left after selling every asset is applied under Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. Immediately after the debts owed to third parties, it goes to pay

options.text_md: each partner rateably what is due to him on account of capital
the realisation expenses of the firm
the residue to the partners in their profit-sharing ratio
each partner rateably what is due to him for advances (loans) to the firm, as distinct from capital

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** each partner rateably what is due to him for advances (loans) to the firm, as distinct from capital. The order is: debts to third parties; then partners' advances (loans) rateably; then partners' capitals rateably; and any residue is divided in the profit-sharing ratio.

questions.stem_md: Under Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the losses of Gopalpur Prawn Farms, an imagined firm being dissolved, including any deficiency of capital, are met

options.text_md: first out of profits, next out of capital, and lastly by the partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio
first out of capital, next out of profits, and lastly by the partners in their capital ratio
by the partners equally, whatever the deed says about sharing profits
out of the partners' loans to the firm before anything else

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** first out of profits, next out of capital, and lastly by the partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio. Section 48(a) uses profits first, then capital, and then calls on the partners individually in the proportion in which they were entitled to share profits.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When the partners of Bhitarkanika Boat Tours, an imagined firm, close the business and settle all its accounts, the partnership among them also comes to an end.

**Reason (R):** Dissolution of the firm ends the relation of partnership among all the partners, not just between some of them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true. Because dissolving the firm ends the relation among every partner, the partnership necessarily ends with it, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On the dissolution of Satpura Safari Lodge, an imagined firm, a loan given to the firm by one of its partners is repaid before any amount is paid to the partners on account of capital.

**Reason (R):** A partner's loan to the firm is an outside liability, so it is transferred to the Realisation Account along with the creditors.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: Section 48 places partners' advances after third-party debts but before capital. R is false: a partner's loan is not an outside liability and never passes through the Realisation Account; it is repaid through the Bank or Cash Account.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When one of the three partners of Lachung Orchid Nursery, an imagined firm, retires and the other two carry on the nursery, the firm is dissolved and its books are closed.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Only the old partnership agreement ends. The firm continues under a new agreement between the two continuing partners, so its books are adjusted for the retirement, not closed.

questions.stem_md: The order in which the cash of Sarangpur Brassware, an imagined firm being wound up, is paid out to creditors, to partners for loans and to partners for capital is laid down in Section ___ of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
questions.solution_md: Section 48 of the Act sets the mode of settlement of accounts between partners after dissolution.

questions.stem_md: Farhana and Jigme, equal partners in Gulmarg Ski Rentals, an imagined firm, close it down. After every asset has been sold, the firm holds ₹1,86,000 in cash. It owes outside creditors ₹80,000 and owes Farhana ₹20,000 on a loan; the capitals are Farhana ₹60,000 and Jigme ₹50,000. How much is finally paid to Jigme on account of his capital (in ₹)?

questions.stem_md: Using Amarkantak Trail Guides, an imagined firm of three partners, as the setting, give two points of difference between dissolution of the partnership and dissolution of the firm.
questions.solution_md: Contrast what happens to the business and to the books in the two cases.

| Basis | Dissolution of partnership | Dissolution of the firm |
|---|---|---|
| Business | Continues: e.g. one guide retires and the other two carry on | Comes to an end: the trail-guide business is closed |
| Books of account | Not closed; adjusted through revaluation, goodwill and capital entries | Closed: assets are realised, liabilities paid and every account settled through the Realisation Account |

questions.stem_md:
Malhar and Nishikant share profits 3 : 1 in Ajanta Cave Tours, an imagined travel firm.

(a) Malhar wants to retire while Nishikant carries on the business; a month later they instead decide to close the business altogether. Explain which of these is a dissolution of the partnership and which a dissolution of the firm, giving one reason each. [2]

(b) On closure, every asset is sold and ₹2,22,000 is available. Creditors are owed ₹90,000, Nishikant's loan to the firm is ₹12,000, and the capitals are Malhar ₹84,000 and Nishikant ₹52,000. Calculate the loss and show the payments in the order required by Section 48. [3]
questions.solution_md: Part (a) turns on whether the business continues; part (b) finds the shortfall, shares it 3 : 1 and pays in the statutory order.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Malhar's retirement with Nishikant carrying on would be a **dissolution of the partnership** only: the old agreement ends, but the firm and its books continue with adjustments. Closing the business altogether is a **dissolution of the firm**: the relation between both partners ends, assets are realised, liabilities paid and the books closed.

**(b)** Loss = (90,000 + 12,000 + 84,000 + 52,000) − 2,22,000 = **₹16,000**, borne 3 : 1: Malhar ₹12,000, Nishikant ₹4,000.

options.text_md: a personal account of the partners that shows their final capitals
a real account that records the cash received from the assets
a nominal account that shows the profit or loss on selling the assets and paying the outside liabilities
a memorandum statement kept outside the double-entry books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a nominal account that shows the profit or loss on selling the assets and paying the outside liabilities. Provision for doubtful debts
Bank overdraft
Trade creditors

credited to the partners' capital accounts in their profit-sharing ratio
debited to the Realisation Account as a loss
deducted from the cash realised from the investments, without any entry

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** credited to the Realisation Account, because the investments it relates to are taken to that account. False

**Reason (R):** A reserve related to no asset or liability belongs to the partners and is credited to their capital accounts in the profit-sharing ratio.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: No entry: the furniture realises nothing

Realisation A/c Dr. To Bank A/c ₹26,000
Bank A/c Dr. To Realisation A/c ₹26,000 (realised at book value)

nil: an intangible asset and a prepaid expense not mentioned are taken to realise nothing
₹14,000 for the patents only
₹3,000 for the prepaid rent only
